baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Challenges a categorical boundary between Indigenous life and modernity through the case of Mary Sully’s art.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary written answer on being native to modernism, 2024. The argument concerns a distinctive artist and does not make her representative of all Indigenous people. The complete book remains unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Explains a collaborative route from family-held drawings through historical research and public talks to museum interpretation.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary Q&A answers on rediscovery, curatorial challenges, book formation and exhibitions. Deloria credits his mother, audiences and named curators; this records historical/public interpretation, not sole creation of the art or a generic museum affiliation.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Deloria criticizes Turner’s frontier boundary for naturalizing Indigenous difference and an expectation of inevitable white triumph (2002).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary publisher excerpt 8–10, with 6–7 framing. Deloria situates Turner within a longer frontier paradigm; this neither makes Turner its sole inventor nor treats all Indigenous historiography as one position. Remaining chapter unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Philip J. Deloria draws on Wilson’s account of oral tradition’s contextual rules and review by knowledgeable audiences when explaining its historical legitimacy (2002).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: A specifically credited methodological resource in Deloria’s own chapter, not a claim of personal mentoring or a general career lineage. He cites Wilson’s 1997 essay, whose body remains unread here; the 1996 essay is a distinct work.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Deloria identifies a tension in Wilson’s oral-history argument between shared practices for checking accuracy and an epistemology that challenges Western historical knowledge (2002).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Qualified methodological reception within his recognition of Native historical authority. His characterization of purity and difference is attributed to him; it does not replace Wilson’s own situated family/community claims or her recorded acknowledgment of archival scholarship’s value and limits.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Deloria incorporates Dickason’s The Myth of the Savage into his account of critical scholarship on the images and discourses that accompanied conquest, crediting its extension to French contexts (2002).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: A named historiographical resource, not personal mentoring or a comprehensive intellectual lineage. Deloria credits Gordon Sayre alongside Dickason. The particular paragraph on p.10 was freshly read and visually checked; Dickason’s book body remains unread. This claim is distinct from Deloria’s already mapped Turner criticism and Wilson resource.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The middle ground: accommodation through mutual invention and creative misunderstanding between Algonquian villages and empires in the Great Lakes region, 1650–1815 (1991)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: White's own statement, The Middle Ground (1991). Introduction, p. ix (Cambridge Core first-page excerpt: the full page, folio observed): histories of Indian–white relations have had 'but two outcomes', stories 'of conquest and assimilation' or 'of cultural persistence'; their tellers 'miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys.' The next page (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi; witnessed only by Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition, page images not seen, the 1991 page inferred) defines the middle ground, in paraphrase, as the space between cultures, between peoples, and between empires and the stateless world of villages, where differences were accommodated through creative and often expedient misunderstanding, and explains it by the long periods in which whites could neither command Indians nor ignore them. Chapter 2 opening (p. 50, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt, folio observed): French and Algonquians 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians.' It rested on 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners' (p. 52), and was, in paraphrase, a product both of everyday life and of formal diplomacy between distinct peoples (p. 53) (both Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition; page numbers as the snippet results give them, taken to match 1991). Chapter 3 opening (p. 94, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): the fur trade was 'a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange'. Epilogue (p. 518, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): 'The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness.' In-period reception, each read in full. Savard (1992; Université de Montréal anthropologist) judges the book's circularity 'inattaquable' and suited to 'bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord', but asks whether the Algonquians' shattered prior state and Iroquois military supremacy, 'cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine', were needed to explain it (p. 120). Edmunds (1993) calls the thesis 'a valuable model for the exploration of the Indian-French relationship' (p. 148) and the book possibly 'a landmark volume in the ethnohistory of the Great Lakes tribes', but finds 'his arguments for the period after 1770 are less convincing' (p. 149). D. R. Miller (1994, Canadian Journal of Native Studies, from the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College) calls it 'an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations' (p. 157), notes that White 'deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian' (p. 158), and writes that 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious' (p. 170). The edge records a scholar's interpretation of Indigenous–imperial relations, which the Indigenous history entry lists as related scholarship; it does not make the work an Indigenous historical practice or a source of Indigenous authority. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: White's 2011 preface (Google Books search-within snippets only) answers Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999; cited pp. xx–xxi) and the later critiques of Havard (Empire et métissages, 2003; p. xvi) and Deloria ('What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', 2006; cited p. xii; both unread here): the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi), and he did not think that 'every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii). McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF) reports that the concept 'struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Deloria criticized the culturally biased social-scientific approach of the workshops McNickle organized, as David Beck’s 1995 history reports.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Program-level criticism, not rejection of all McNickle’s writing. Beck identifies Deloria as a guest speaker at the 1965 workshop and one of its critics, citing Dorothy Parker (1992), p. 195; that book and Deloria’s original statement remain unread. Douglas Miller’s 2016 review separately describes a widening ideological gulf, while challenging a dismissive account of McNickle. Neither source establishes McNickle as Deloria’s mentor.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Calloway identifies Deloria’s critique of outside experts as a continuing caution for his own practice and accountability to Native communities.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Own interview section3 explicitly includes himself among non-Native researchers made to reconsider their methods. The1969 collection remains unread; this is acknowledged methodological use, not an inference about Indigenous identity.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Native Studies does not belong under Ethnic Studies: to 'classify us as just another ethnic minority, it is colonialist'; 'we are not an ethnic minority … We are Indigenous', and 'Fourth World Studies is the next logical step' for comparison (1998; first given at UBC in 1995).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998): p. 33 (Native Studies 'does not belong under the rubric of Ethnic Studies'), p. 36 (Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins on lumping minority groups together), pp. 34–38 (Blauner's colonial model, whose conclusion she accepts while criticising his evidence), p. 40 ('colonialist'), p. 49 (conclusion). First presented at UBC, 2 November 1995 (p. 50 note). Protocol passages (pp. 38–39) are not used (OCAP).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Wheeler opens her case that Indigenous peoples are not an ethnic minority with Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins (1969) on liberals who 'categorize them all together' as minority groups, and returns to him on cooperative movements (1998).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998), p. 36 (Deloria quoted, notes 6–9) and pp. 46–47 (Deloria 1969 on cooperative movements).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Coulthard grounds his place-based critique in God Is Red: Deloria's 'distinction between Indigenous place-based and Western time-oriented understandings of the world' (2009)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 88 (read): Deloria's 'groundbreaking 1972 text, God is Red' holds that Western societies derive meaning 'in historical/developmental terms, thereby placing time as the narrative of central importance'; the quoted distinction is Coulthard's own wording; p. 89: land as a field of 'relationships of things to each other' (quoting Deloria 2001). The passage that follows, on Dene relations to land, is community knowledge and is not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked.
